theme: Orientation — I don't know where to start
theme_description: The pain of not yet having an evaluation programme. The team can ship an LLM feature but cannot defensibly answer "is this working?" — no dataset, no monitoring discipline, no shared vocabulary, no way to tell whether a change made things better or worse.
problem: Don't know where to start an eval suite
problem_description: The team agrees they need evals but has no entry point — no canonical dataset, no agreed task shape, no decision on graders. Work stalls at the first design meeting.
action: Start with 20–50 tasks drawn from real failure transcripts; combine code-based, model-based, and human graders; manage non-determinism with pass@k and pass^k

theme_description: The pain of an organisation that builds the same thing repeatedly. Every team rebuilds eval scaffolding, prompts proliferate inconsistently, skill registries are maintained by hand, repo-by-repo upgrades crawl, and the 80→95 quality plateau eats most of the budget.
problem: Mixing capability and regression testing into one suite
problem_description: One eval set tries to answer both "what can this agent do" and "has anything broken since last week." The two questions need different cadences and signal profiles; conflating them produces a suite that does neither well.
action: Separate capability evals (exploring what the agent can do) from regression evals (catching breaks) — they have different shapes and cadences

theme_description: The pain of high scores that don't predict real outcomes. Coding agents pass shallow checks but fail in practice; healthcare benchmarks fixate on accuracy; "agent did X% of work" headlines hide that full delegation success is closer to 0–20%. The metric and the goal have decoupled.
problem: Coding/computer-use agents that pass shallow checks but fail in practice
problem_description: Tests assert that an output looks right (compiles, returns JSON, clicks the button) but never check the underlying state or behaviour. Agents reliably pass these tests and reliably fail in production.
action: For coding agents: deterministic outcome tests + LLM rubrics for code quality. For computer-use: verify both UI actions and backend state

theme: Observability — can I see what happened?
theme_description: The pain of not being able to see what an agent actually did. Logs are partial, traces aren't comparable across frameworks, long runs hide their failure point, and tool calls and reasoning steps disappear into a black box. Post-hoc debugging is impossible without instrumentation the team didn't install in time.
problem_description: Tests fire at individual model calls or tool calls but never grade the trajectory as a whole. Workflow-level failures (skipped step, wrong handoff, lost context) slip through.
action: Frame each eval as `prompt → captured run (trace + artifacts) → checks → comparable score`; have structured graders score traces against criteria covering model calls, tool calls, guardrails, and handoffs

theme: Trust the scores — variance, bias, calibration
theme_description: The pain of measurement validity. Single-run scores look stable but aren't; LLM-judge scores drift between models, across versions, and against humans; standard errors are absent or computed wrong. The team cannot tell whether a score change reflects a real improvement or noise.
problem: LLM-judge scores aren't trustworthy across studies
problem_description: Two write-ups report "LLM-judge score X" with no calibration data. The numbers can't be compared — one judge may run 30 points stricter than another on the same outputs.
action: Calibrate judges to ≥0.80 Spearman correlation with human evaluators before treating scores as comparable

problem_description: The judge consistently prefers longer answers, or first-position answers, or its own model family's style. The rubric measures what the judge likes, not what the rubric is supposed to measure.
action: Use evidence-anchored scoring and ensemble methods (multiple judges, position/length bias mitigations)

problem_description: Reasoning quality and task success are conflated into one score. A good plan followed by a bad final answer looks the same as a bad plan that happened to succeed.
action: Split metrics into trajectory (reasoning steps, tool selection, decision paths) and outcome (completion, accuracy, latency) — measure both

problem_description: Team plans to fix production issues by upgrading to a smarter model. The real binding constraint is capacity, runtime, or prompt caching — none of which a better model solves.
action: Plan capacity and observability first — ~5% of AI requests fail in production, ~60% from capacity limits, not model quality

action: Optimize system architecture before backend model choice or tool config — architecture dominates for resource use, reproducibility, and performance

problem_description: Adopting an LLM-as-judge product and reporting its scores as ground truth, without ever measuring how the judge agrees with a human on the team's own data.

problem: Synthetic benchmarks diverge from real usage
problem_description: Test set was generated by an LLM or hand-crafted; production traffic looks completely different in length, structure, vocabulary, and intent.
action: Build benchmarks from real developer-agent sessions: verbatim prompt + committed change + fail-to-pass tests; add multi-run stability checks for noisy monorepos

problem: Treating offline scores as ground truth
problem_description: A benchmark number went up, so the change ships. The offline number was never validated against an A/B comparison, and the production effect is unknown.
action: Complement offline signals with online A/B tests before production go/no-go decisions

problem: Ignoring cost and business-value in eval
problem_description: The eval reports accuracy only. Two options at the same accuracy might differ in cost by an order of magnitude, but the team's leaderboard hides that.
action: Measure cost/business-value alongside quality — 40% of agentic AI projects projected to be cancelled by 2027 over unclear value/rising costs

problem_description: Adding subagents made things worse, not better. The team can't explain why and is considering reverting to a single agent.
action: Use multi-agents only where they work: (a) code-review loops with a separate reviewer agent (~2 bugs/PR caught, 58% severe), (b) smart-friend escalation, (c) hierarchical delegation for week-long tasks. Keep writes single-threaded

problem: Don't know how many eval questions you need
problem_description: Picked 100 questions because that's how many fit on a screen. Whether 100 is enough to detect the gap they care about is unaddressed.
action: Run a power analysis: `n = ((z_{α/2} + z_β)² · variance_term) / δ²`; size for the smallest gap you care about (e.g. 3 pp at power 0.8)

theme: Trust the scores — variance, bias, calibration
theme_description: The pain of measurement validity. Single-run scores look stable but aren't; LLM-judge scores drift between models, across versions, and against humans; standard errors are absent or computed wrong. The team cannot tell whether a score change reflects a real improvement or noise.
problem: Tiny eval sets used with CLT-style stats
problem_description: 50 examples, 95% confidence interval calculated with the central limit theorem. The CIs are unreliable below ~100 datapoints.
action: Don't apply CLT below ~100 datapoints (use Bayesian alternatives); prefer continuous metrics (token likelihoods) over binary correctness

theme: Orientation — I don't know where to start
theme_description: The pain of not yet having an evaluation programme. The team can ship an LLM feature but cannot defensibly answer "is this working?" — no dataset, no monitoring discipline, no shared vocabulary, no way to tell whether a change made things better or worse.
problem: Picking the right statistical test per eval
problem_description: For continuous, paired, ordinal, multi-comparison data: which test? Most teams default to whatever stats-101 procedure they remember.
action: Use the `evalstats` Python library (statsforevals.com) to auto-select methods; apply multiple-comparison corrections; use sequential hypothesis testing for iterative dev; report effect sizes — only 16% of 445 surveyed benchmarks ran any statistical test

theme_description: The pain of being a target. Prompt injection, the lethal trifecta (private data + injection + exfiltration), agent goal hijack, privilege escalation, tool misuse — and the team has no agent-specific threat model or red-team programme.
problem_description: OWASP Top 10 for LLMs covers prompt injection but not goal hijack, tool misuse, agent-to-agent comms. The team's threat model is a year out of date.
action: Threat-model against the OWASP ASI Top 10: Goal Hijack, Tool Misuse, Identity/Privilege Abuse, Supply Chain, Code Execution, Memory/Context Poisoning, Inter-Agent Comms, Cascading Failures, Human-Agent Trust, Rogue Agents

theme_description: The pain of being a target. Prompt injection, the lethal trifecta (private data + injection + exfiltration), agent goal hijack, privilege escalation, tool misuse — and the team has no agent-specific threat model or red-team programme.
problem_description: What does "red-team the agent" mean? Multi-step trajectories? Inter-agent channels? Tool boundaries? No agreed scope.
action: Define red-team scope across multi-step trajectories, tool boundaries, and agent-to-agent communication channels; collect evidence mapped to enterprise audit requirements

theme: Observability — can I see what happened?
theme_description: The pain of not being able to see what an agent actually did. Logs are partial, traces aren't comparable across frameworks, long runs hide their failure point, and tool calls and reasoning steps disappear into a black box. Post-hoc debugging is impossible without instrumentation the team didn't install in time.
problem: Hard to trace what an OpenAI Agents/Codex skill actually did
problem_description: Skill ran. Output looks weird. Logs offer little; the team can't reconstruct what the skill chose to do, step by step.
action: Use `codex exec --json --full-auto` to emit a JSONL event stream you can grade against

action: Use next-token log-probabilities instead of sampling — ~67% variance reduction for single-token answers
